summary.text: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that an independent outcome that has come up less often than expected is more likely to happen next, or the reverse.
With a fair coin, the chance of heads on the next toss is 1/2 however long the run before it, because past results carry no memory.
It is also called the Monte Carlo fallacy, after 1913 when a roulette wheel landed on black 26 times in a row and gamblers lost millions of francs betting against black.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Monte Carlo fallacy; fallacy of the maturity of chances

facts.label: Monte Carlo 1913
facts.value: A roulette ball fell on black 26 times in a row

facts.label: Equal sequences
facts.value: 21 heads and 20 heads then a tail are equally likely

facts.label: Early description
facts.value: Laplace described it in 1796, in a case about births of boys and girls

facts.label: Where it fails
facts.value: It does not apply when events are not independent

items.prompt: A friend has just flipped a fair coin and got heads four times. She says tails is now due. What is the chance of tails on the fifth flip?

options.label: More than 1/2, since the run must balance out
Less than 1/2, since heads is on a hot streak
1/2, the same as on any other flip
1/32, since a run of five is rare

items.explain: The chance of a long run is small only before the tosses; once four are done, the next toss is still 1/2 and past heads do not influence it.

items.prompt: You will flip a fair coin 21 times. Which outcome is more likely: 21 heads, or 20 heads followed by a tail?

options.label: 21 heads, since a streak that long looks more lawful
20 heads then a tail, since the streak must end sometime
Neither is more likely, since every sequence of 21 flips is equally likely
It depends on how many heads came in earlier games

items.explain: Every 21-flip sequence has the same probability, 1 in 2,097,152, so assuming a change after earlier flips is a mistake.

items.prompt: You draw an ace from a standard deck and set it aside. Compared with before, how likely is the next card to be an ace?

options.label: Less likely, since one of the aces is now gone
More likely, since aces are due to appear
Equally likely, since each card is a fresh trial
Impossible to tell without counting the jokers

items.explain: The gambler's fallacy does not apply here because drawing without replacement makes the events not independent: the chance of another ace falls from 4/52 to 3/51.

items.prompt: A roulette wheel has landed on black many times in a row. A bettor piles money on red, reasoning that the wheel must even itself out. What is wrong with that thinking?

options.label: Red has no chance of ending the streak, so the bet is lost already
Streaks like this mean the wheel is surely broken in favour of black
The wheel is more likely to stay black until the casino resets it
The streak creates no imbalance, so each spin keeps its usual chances

items.explain: The gamblers at Monte Carlo reasoned wrongly that the streak was causing an imbalance in the wheel's randomness; for an unbiased wheel each spin is independent.

items.prompt: After a coin has landed tails many times in a row, a gambler starts to think the coin may be biased towards tails. Is this the gambler's fallacy?

options.label: Yes, since any change in belief after a streak is a fallacy
Yes, since a fair coin has no way to show a streak
No, since a streak of heads would be equally unusual
No, since doubting the coin is fair is a reasonable conclusion

items.explain: Concluding that tails is favoured because the coin may not be fair is rational and Bayesian. The fallacy is believing a sequence of fair trials remembers past results.

items.prompt: Several families in a neighbourhood have just had baby boys. An expectant father reasons that those boys make a girl more probable for his own baby. How should this be described?

options.label: Sound, since births must match up month by month
The gambler's fallacy, since past births do not shift the odds of the next
Sound, since fewer boys remain to be born
A new idea, since births cannot be compared with coin flips

items.explain: Laplace described fathers who thought boys already born made girls more probable next, among the earliest descriptions of the fallacy.
